quote: Die erste Frage ist: wie vieldeu= tig ist die Funktion, welche [-jenes-] das gegebene Verzweigungsgebilde mit den gegebenen Perioden besitzt d.h. wie vielfach muss ich den Raum überdecken
english: The first question is: how many-valued is the function which has the given branching locus with the given periods, i.e. how many times must I cover the space
topic: On cutting a space by sections so that it becomes simply connected, constructing functions with a given branching locus composed of irreducible components with given periods, and asking how many-valued such a function must be.

triage.modern_statement: Let X be a complex space, e.g. C^n or P^n, and let D be a hypersurface (the 'branching locus') with irreducible components D_1,…,D_k. To each D_i assign a 'period', meaning the local monodromy or ramification order around D_i. The question is whether there is a connected finite branched covering Y→X, i.e. an algebraic or analytic multivalued function, that is branched exactly along D with the prescribed periods. If so, what is the smallest number of sheets ('how many times must I cover the space')? In modern terms the coverings correspond to transitive permutation representations of π1(X∖D), so the minimal degree is the smallest index of a finite-index subgroup that is compatible with the prescribed monodromy orders around the meridians of the D_i. Whether a finite cover extends across D is answered by the higher-dimensional Riemann existence theorem.
triage.answered_by: No single answer exists, because the minimal sheet number depends on the specific branch locus. The framework was settled in two steps. Oscar Zariski (1929, Amer. J. Math., 'On the problem of existence of algebraic functions of two variables possessing a given branch curve') reduced the existence question for plane branch curves to the fundamental group of the complement, which became the theory of Zariski pairs and of fundamental groups of curve complements. Grauert and Remmert (1958) proved the higher-dimensional Riemann existence theorem: finite unramified covers of the complement of a hypersurface extend to normal analytic, and in the projective case algebraic, branched covers. Together these reduce Hilbert's question to the group theory of π1(X∖D). Computing that group for a given D is still done case by case.

evidence.claim: Zariski's 1929 paper asked whether an algebraic function of x and y exists with a preassigned curve as its branch curve. This is the same question as Hilbert's note, for surfaces. The survey 'A survey on Zariski pairs' treats this paper as the origin of the Zariski-pairs topic.

Harbater's survey of Riemann's Existence Theorem says that [GrRe58] (Grauert–Remmert 1958) extended the theorem to higher dimensions. That result links branched covers with a given branch locus to finite covers of the complement, and so to the fundamental group.
A biography of Grauert notes that one of the most quoted Grauert–Remmert theorems is about extending covers over a complement in higher dimensions.
Nori's 1983 work 'Zariski's conjecture and related problems' cites Zariski's branch-curve paper and studies when the fundamental group of the complement of a divisor is abelian.
Work on Zariski multiples and Zariski pairs of branch curves continues; there are 2025 and 2026 papers citing Zariski's 1929 branch-curve paper.

triage.why: The note asks about the existence and minimal sheet number of a multivalued function with a prescribed branch locus and prescribed periods. That is the higher-dimensional version of the Riemann existence problem. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Grauert–Remmert (1958) answered the general existence and extension question. Zariski (1929) showed that for plane curves the answer depends on π1 of the complement, so the number of sheets depends on the specific locus and has no closed-form answer. The research Zariski started (fundamental groups of complements, Zariski pairs and multiples) is still active. I found no source showing that Hilbert's note directly influenced Zariski or Grauert–Remmert; the link is only that they address the same mathematical question. Confidence is medium because the note is brief, so reading 'periods' as monodromy or ramification data is my interpretation.
